title: The village
hook: he walked to town often; Walden was a short walk from Concord, and his mother fed him sometimes

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bean field: Thoreau set out to know beans, and found the harvest was partly the woodchucks'. Your line was to know beans. What did you tend, and did it hurry for you? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-three.

"Every day or two I strolled to the village to hear some of the gossip." That's Thoreau, in Walden, the book known as the story of a man alone in the woods. And there it is, in his own words: every day or two, a walk into town. Not a secret he got caught keeping. He gave it a chapter of its own, right in the middle of the book, and called it The Village. So today, a gentler picture of the hermit. The cabin was real. So was the path out of the woods.
screen: `EVERY DAY OR TWO.` → `A CHAPTER CALLED THE VILLAGE.` → `THE PATH OUT OF THE WOODS.`

segments.voice: First, the setup. Walden opens with Thoreau telling us he lived alone, in the woods, "a mile from any neighbor," in a house he built himself. That's the picture that sticks. A mile is real distance on foot. It is also a walk you can make before lunch. Second, what he went for. In The Village he says he went to hear the gossip, and that taken in small doses it was as refreshing in its own way as the rustle of leaves and the peeping of frogs. He's not apologizing. He's saying people are part of the landscape too. He watched the villagers the way he watched the pond. Third, the walk home. He describes leaving town late, sometimes on dark nights, and finding his way back through the woods by feel, his feet knowing the path when his eyes couldn't. The village and the woods weren't two worlds. They were two ends of one walk. Fourth, the help. Some readers like to point out, sometimes as a joke at his expense, that his family's house in Concord was close by, and tradition says he ate there now and then. It's easy to make that a gotcha: some hermit. But there's another way to hear it. Nobody really lives alone. Thoreau's experiment in living simply still had a mother, a town, a cobbler and a road under it. Being honest about that doesn't shrink the experiment. It makes it something an ordinary person could try.
screen: `A MILE FROM ANY NEIGHBOR.` · `GOSSIP IN SMALL DOSES.` · `HOME BY FEEL IN THE DARK.` · then, large: `NOBODY REALLY LIVES ALONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be honest about your support. Sit comfortably, and breathe. Then, quietly, start counting what holds you up. Not in a grand way. The person who taught you to cook, or the one who still does. The friend who answers late. The bus driver. The water that comes out of the tap. The shop that has bread. Let each one come and go with a breath. If you pray, you can hold them there for a moment. There's no need to feel anything in particular. Just notice how long the list gets. The bell holds the time.
The village. Thoreau lived a mile from any neighbor, and still walked into Concord every day or two, for the gossip and the company. Today's word.
Your line: not so alone. Today, pick one name from your list and let them know, in a word or a message, that they're part of what holds you up. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Readers of Walden often notice that Thoreau's solitude sat close to a town he visited often, and take it as a reminder that even a simple, independent life rests on other people.
